criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

Vignette:
Mr. E is a 26 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, headache, and non-productive cough. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat. He has been afebrile. His physical examination is normal, except for some pharyngeal erythema. He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for acetaminophen for his sore throat and fever. He has no drug allergies.
winner_protocol:
Age: 26
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sore throat, headache, and non-productive cough of 2 days' duration, with acute onset of sore throat; patient is afebrile and otherwise in good health.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with an acute viral upper respiratory infection (viral pharyngitis/common cold). Supporting facts include the acute onset of sore throat, headache, non-productive cough, afebrile status, and a normal physical examination except for pharyngeal erythema. The absence of fever, tonsillar exudates, and cervical lymphadenopathy makes a bacterial etiology (e.g., Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis) less likely. Main differential considerations include Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis, influenza, COVID-19, and allergic rhinitis/post-nasal drip. The patient is stable with no red flags, and the condition is expected to be self-limited.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None routinely indicated. Consider COVID-19 testing if there is known exposure or high community transmission; consider rapid strep test or throat culture only if clinical suspicion for bacterial infection rises (e.g., development of fever, exudates, or lymphadenopathy).
Conclusion: This is a self-limited viral upper respiratory infection appropriate for symptomatic management and self-care. No emergent care or specialist referral is needed at this time. The patient should be advised on return precautions and preventive measures.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Provide symptomatic care with rest, adequate hydration, and acetaminophen for pain/fever; throat lozenges or warm salt-water gargles may help. Avoid aspirin due to Reye's syndrome risk. Antibiotics are not indicated. Educate the patient on the expected duration of 7-10 days and the viral nature of the illness. Advise return precautions: seek care if high fever, difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, muffled voice, stridor, neck stiffness, severe headache, rash, or symptoms persisting beyond 7-10 days. Emphasize hand hygiene and cough etiquette to prevent transmission. Obtain exposure history to sick contacts (COVID-19, influenza, strep) and clarify vaccination status (influenza, COVID-19). Inquire about smoking/vaping, travel history, allergy history, recent antibiotic use, and immunosuppressive conditions. Note the discrepancy that the patient takes acetaminophen for "sore throat and fever" despite being reported afebrile; fever may be masked by the antipyretic. Consider mononucleosis evaluation if symptoms persist or if significant fatigue, lymphadenopathy, or tonsillar exudates develop later. Ensure the patient is up-to-date on vaccinations. Routine follow-up with primary care; ENT referral only if symptoms persist beyond 10 days or complications develop.
Notes: The absence of fever is reassuring but does not entirely exclude bacterial infection; clinical judgment is needed. The patient's acetaminophen use may mask fever, so this should be clarified. None.

Diagnosis10: Acute transmural myocardial infarction of anterior wall
Vignette: Mr. Y is a 64 year old Chinese male who presents with chest pain for 24 hours. One day prior to presentation, the patient began to experience 8/10, non-radiating substernal chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. The pain intially improved with Tylenol, however over the following 24 hours, his symptoms worsened. The patient went to his primary physician, where an EKG was performed which showed ST elevation in leads V2-V6.
Simplified (added symptoms): 64 y/o m, 1 day chest pain (8/10), non-radiating substernal chest pressure, sweating, shortness of breath, (chest tightness)

points: 10
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Recognizes anterolateral STEMI (ST elevation V2-V6) as a time-critical emergency requiring immediate activation of cath lab for primary PCI (door-to-balloon time less than 90 minutes).

[2]
points: 9
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Interprets ECG findings correctly: ST elevation in V2-V6 indicates extensive anterior wall MI (likely LAD occlusion), with significant risk of LV dysfunction and complications.

[3]
points: 9
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Recommends immediate initial treatment: aspirin 162-325 mg chewed, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation (heparin), nitrates if not hypotensive, and morphine for pain if needed.

[4]
points: 8
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Highlights that 24-hour symptom duration extends but does not eliminate benefit of reperfusion; PCI is still indicated, especially with ongoing symptoms or hemodynamic instability.

[5]
points: 7
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Orders appropriate workup: serial troponins, CBC, basic metabolic panel, coagulation studies, lipid panel, CXR, and bedside echocardiogram to assess LV function and mechanical complications.

[6]
points: 6
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Considers and addresses STEMI mimics (pericarditis, early repolarization, LV aneurysm, Takotsubo) but recognizes the classic presentation here strongly supports MI.

[7]
points: 6
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Monitors for and addresses complications: arrhythmias (VF/VT), cardiogenic shock, mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture), and heart failure.

[8]
points: 5
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Discusses post-PCI care: guideline-directed medical therapy (dual antiplatelet, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, high-intensity statin), cardiac rehab, and risk factor modification.

[9]
points: 4
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Asks about prior cardiac history, medications, allergies (especially contrast/aspirin), bleeding risk, and recent surgeries before anticoagulation.

[10]
points: -10
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Penalize failing to recognize STEMI urgency or delaying reperfusion in favor of conservative/outpatient management.

[11]
points: -8
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Penalize misinterpreting the ECG (e.g., diagnosing pericarditis without distinguishing features, or non-STEMI).

[12]
points: -6
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Penalize omitting dual antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation in initial management.

[13]
points: -4
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Penalize dwelling on differential diagnoses (such as MSK pain or GERD) at the expense of timely reperfusion.

Vignette:
Mr. Y is a 64 year old Chinese male who presents with chest pain for 24 hours. One day prior to presentation, the patient began to experience 8/10, non-radiating substernal chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. The pain intially improved with Tylenol, however over the following 24 hours, his symptoms worsened. The patient went to his primary physician, where an EKG was performed which showed ST elevation in leads V2-V6.
winner_protocol:
Age: 64 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: 24-hour history of worsening 8/10 non-radiating substernal chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath; EKG performed by primary physician shows ST elevation in leads V2-V6.

Analysis: The clinical presentation of substernal chest pressure with diaphoresis and dyspnea, combined with ST elevation in contiguous precordial leads V2-V6, is classic for an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), most likely due to occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. This is a time-critical emergency in which "time is muscle"; delays in reperfusion increase myocardial necrosis and mortality. The 24-hour symptom duration places the patient beyond the optimal 12-hour reperfusion window, but reperfusion is still indicated given ongoing symptoms and evidence of ongoing ischemia. The initial improvement with Tylenol does not rule out cardiac ischemia. Main differential considerations that must be actively excluded before initiating antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy include aortic dissection with coronary involvement, acute pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, and esophageal rupture; however, the clinical picture and EKG findings strongly favor anterior STEMI. Red flags include severe chest pain, diaphoresis, dyspnea, age >60, widespread anterior ST elevation, and prolonged symptom duration, all indicating high-risk ACS with risk of malignant arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and mechanical complications.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin; repeat 12-lead EKG; right-sided EKG (V4R) to assess right ventricular involvement; continuous ECG monitoring; portable chest X-ray; complete blood count; basic metabolic panel (including baseline renal function before contrast administration); coagulation profile; lipid panel; bedside transthoracic echocardiogram to assess left ventricular function and exclude mechanical complications; blood pressure measurement in both arms and pulse checks to exclude aortic dissection; emergent coronary angiography with primary PCI capability.

Conclusion: This is a time-critical anterior STEMI (likely LAD occlusion) in a 64-year-old male presenting with 24 hours of worsening ischemic chest pain and ST elevation in V2-V6. The patient requires immediate emergent care with cardiology consultation, activation of the catheterization lab, and urgent reperfusion therapy (primary PCI preferred; fibrinolysis if PCI not available within guideline-specified time), along with standard adjunctive medical therapy and close monitoring for complications.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Cardiology

Recommendations: Activate the STEMI protocol immediately. Administer chewable aspirin 162-325 mg, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g., ticagrelor or prasugrel; clopidogrel 600 mg as alternative), and anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin (or bivalirudin). Give sublingual nitroglycerin if no hypotension or right ventricular involvement is suspected; use high-flow oxygen only if oxygen saturation <94%. Consider a beta-blocker if no contraindication. Arrange emergent primary PCI as the preferred reperfusion strategy; if PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes, screen for contraindications and administer fibrinolytic therapy. Assess hemodynamic stability (blood pressure, heart rate, signs of cardiogenic shock) as vital signs are not provided. Actively exclude aortic dissection by checking blood pressure differentials and pulses before initiating antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy. Obtain cardiac biomarkers (troponin) to confirm and risk-stratify the MI. Document traditional cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, family history) for risk stratification. Assess baseline renal function before contrast administration during PCI. Consider right ventricular involvement with a right-sided EKG (V4R) given the anterior MI. Ensure continuous cardiac monitoring given the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Monitor for post-MI complications including arrhythmias, heart failure, and mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture, free wall rupture). Transfer to a PCI-capable center if not available. After reperfusion, transfer to a cardiac intensive care unit for monitoring, initiate secondary-prevention medications (high-intensity statin, ACE-I/ARB, beta-blocker, continued antiplatelet therapy), assess left ventricular function with echocardiography, and arrange cardiac rehabilitation and outpatient follow-up. Address cultural considerations: assess for language barriers, health literacy, and preferences for traditional medicine, which may affect consent and adherence.

Notes: The 24-hour symptom duration increases the risk of complications and may limit the benefit of reperfusion; this should be factored into decision-making, though ongoing ischemia still warrants reperfusion. Vital signs are not provided, so hemodynamic status must be assessed on arrival. Initial improvement with Tylenol does not rule out cardiac ischemia.

The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.

winner_protocol:
Age: 15 years old

Sex: Female

Complaint: Superficial scrape on the left knee after falling off a skateboard onto pavement approximately 1 hour prior; wound was cleaned with water at home.

Analysis: The patient presents with a 6 by 4 cm superficial abrasion on the anterior left knee following a fall onto pavement. Examination shows minor oozing of serous fluid, no active arterial bleeding, no embedded foreign material visible, no deeper tissue involvement, intact surrounding skin, and full painless range of motion of the knee. There is no history of head strike, loss of consciousness, or other injuries, and tetanus immunization is up to date. These findings are consistent with a benign superficial abrasion. Differential considerations include superficial laceration, contusion, retained foreign body, occult fracture, early cellulitis, and (rarely) septic arthritis, but all are less likely given the benign examination. No red flags such as active bleeding, deep tissue involvement, neurovascular compromise, or functional impairment are present. The condition is non-urgent and appropriate for self-care or primary care management; no diagnostic imaging or laboratory testing is indicated.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None

Conclusion: This is a minor, superficial abrasion of the left knee with no signs of complication. The injury is non-urgent and self-care appropriate, requiring only wound cleansing, topical antibiotic application, sterile dressing, and monitoring for signs of infection. No tetanus booster is needed given up-to-date immunization, and no diagnostic investigations are warranted.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Recommendations: 
- Gently irrigate the wound with sterile saline or clean water to remove any residual debris; although the patient already cleaned it with water at home, further irrigation is prudent, and careful inspection for tiny embedded particulate matter from pavement is advised to prevent tattooing or infection.
- Apply a topical antibiotic ointment and cover with a sterile dressing; change the dressing daily and keep the wound clean and dry.
- No tetanus booster is required, but verify the exact date of the last booster to ensure it is within the recommended 5–10 years for a dirty wound.
- No prophylactic antibiotics are needed unless signs of infection develop, given the clean and superficial nature of the wound.
- Use over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) if needed, though pain is minimal.
- Monitor for signs of infection (redness, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, fever) and return if there is no improvement within 3–5 days or if symptoms worsen.
- Limit activities that cause friction on the wound for 24–48 hours to promote healing and prevent re-injury.
- Provide adolescent-specific education, including safety gear use (e.g., knee pads) while skateboarding, and assess the patient's ability to adhere to wound-care instructions.
- Consider discussing potential scar formation and cosmetic concerns, especially in an adolescent, and note environmental factors such as dirt, oil, or chemicals on pavement that may increase infection risk.

Notes: None

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. - a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man with hypertension and degenerative joint disease presents to the emergency department with a three-day history of a productive cough and fever. He has a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F), a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 92 percent while breathing room air. Physical examination reveals only crackles and egophony in the right lower lung field. The white-cell count is 14,000 per cubic millimeter, and the results of routine chemical tests are normal. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe.
winner_protocol:
Age: 65 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: Three-day history of productive cough and fever, with hypoxemia (oxygen saturation 92% on room air) and a right lower lobe infiltrate on chest radiograph.

Analysis: The patient presents with a classic picture of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP): productive cough, fever (38.3°C), tachypnea (RR 22), crackles and egophony in the right lower lung field, leukocytosis (WBC 14,000/µL), and a right lower lobe infiltrate on chest radiograph. The oxygen saturation of 92% on room air indicates mild hypoxemia, which is a severity marker and warrants emergent evaluation and treatment. His age (65 years) and comorbid hypertension further increase his risk for complications. The main differential considerations include bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, atypical organisms) and, less likely, other causes of lobar infiltrate such as aspiration pneumonia or a post-obstructive process. The findings do not suggest heart failure (no mention of jugular venous distension, edema, or diffuse findings) or pulmonary embolism (no acute pleuritic chest pain or risk factors specified). Severity scoring (e.g., CURB-65 or PSI) is not provided but would be appropriate to guide disposition; based on the available data (age, hypoxemia), hospitalization is warranted.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pulse oximetry (already performed, showing 92% on room air; repeat as needed); arterial blood gas (to assess oxygenation and acid-base status if clinically indicated); sputum Gram stain and culture; blood cultures (before antibiotics); complete blood count with differential (already done); serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose (routine chemistry already normal, but repeat if clinically indicated); chest radiograph (already done); consider procalcitonin or CRP if available; assess for influenza and other respiratory viral testing if seasonally appropriate.

Conclusion: This is a 65-year-old man with hypertension presenting with community-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe, complicated by mild hypoxemia (SpO2 92% on room air). Given his age, comorbidity, and oxygen requirement, he requires emergent care, hospital admission, and initiation of empiric antibiotic therapy, with ongoing monitoring of oxygenation and response to treatment.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology

Recommendations: Admit the patient to the hospital for management of community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxemia. Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy covering typical and atypical pathogens (e.g., a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone, per local guidelines and allergy status). Administer supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 92% (or per institutional target). Obtain blood cultures and sputum cultures before starting antibiotics. Assess pneumonia severity using a validated tool (e.g., CURB-65 or PSI) to guide disposition and monitoring. Monitor vital signs, oxygenation, and clinical response; reassess for need for escalation of respiratory support (e.g., noninvasive ventilation or ICU care) if hypoxemia worsens. Evaluate for complications such as parapneumonic effusion or empyema with repeat imaging if clinically indicated. Ensure adequate hydration and antipyretics for fever. Address vaccination status (influenza, pneumococcal) and provide smoking cessation counseling if applicable. Arrange follow-up chest radiograph in 6–8 weeks to document resolution, particularly given his age and comorbidity.

Notes: The patient's oxygen saturation of 92% on room air is a key severity indicator and justifies emergent care and hospitalization. Antibiotic selection should be guided by local resistance patterns, patient allergies, and severity; duration typically 5–7 days for uncomplicated CAP if clinically stable. If the patient deteriorates or fails to improve within 48–72 hours, reassess for alternative diagnoses or complications. Not specified: vaccination status, smoking history, prior antibiotic use, or allergy history.

Vignette:
A 33-year-old man presents with a several-month history of persistent flaky, scaly patches on his scalp and eyebrows. He reports mild itching that is worse after showering. He has tried regular shampoo without improvement. He denies hair loss, spreading to other body areas, or any joint symptoms. He has no history of psoriasis or HIV. On examination, there are yellowish, greasy scales on the scalp, particularly along the hairline and in the eyebrow region. Mild erythema underlies the scales. There are no excoriations or signs of secondary infection.
winner_protocol:
Age: 33
Sex: Male
Complaint: Persistent flaky, scaly patches on the scalp and eyebrows with mild itching that worsens after showering; no improvement with regular shampoo.
Analysis: The patient presents with a several-month history of yellowish, greasy scales on the scalp (particularly along the hairline) and in the eyebrow region, with mild underlying erythema and mild itching. These findings are classic for seborrheic dermatitis. The absence of hair loss, spreading to other body areas, joint symptoms, excoriations, or signs of secondary infection, along with no history of psoriasis or HIV, supports this diagnosis and lowers concern for more serious conditions. The main differential considerations include scalp psoriasis, tinea capitis/faciei, atopic dermatitis, and contact dermatitis; however, the greasy quality of the scales and the characteristic distribution favor seborrheic dermatitis over these alternatives. The lack of response to regular shampoo suggests the need for medicated, prescription-strength products targeting Malassezia yeast overgrowth and the associated inflammation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical and no routine laboratory tests or imaging are required. If the condition is atypical, refractory, or tinea is strongly suspected, a KOH preparation or fungal culture could be considered; a skin biopsy is reserved for uncertain cases.
Conclusion: This is a classic presentation of seborrheic dermatitis, a chronic, non-urgent dermatologic condition. The patient has no red flags (no hair loss, no systemic symptoms, no joint pain, no rapid spread, no secondary infection, no immunosuppression history). Management is outpatient and focuses on reducing Malassezia colonization and controlling inflammation with medicated shampoos and low-potency topical anti-inflammatory agents, with follow-up in 4–6 weeks.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: 
- Initiate a medicated antifungal shampoo (e.g., ketoconazole 2%, selenium sulfide, or zinc pyrithione) used 2–3 times weekly, leaving it on the scalp for several minutes before rinsing.
- For the eyebrows and facial involvement, apply a low-potency topical corticosteroid or a topical calcineurin inhibitor short-term for flare-ups, along with gentle emollients/moisturizers.
- Advise gentle cleansing and avoidance of harsh hair products; regular shampoo lacks antifungal or keratolytic activity, explaining the lack of response.
- Educate the patient to avoid scratching to prevent secondary bacterial infection; current skin integrity is good with no excoriations.
- Consider asking about eye symptoms (e.g., redness, burning) to assess for concomitant blepharitis, given eyebrow involvement; advise eyelid hygiene if present.
- Discuss potential triggers (stress, cold/dry weather, fatigue, oily skin) and the association with Malassezia overgrowth; male sex and age 30–60 are risk factors present in this case.
- Limit the duration and potency of topical corticosteroids on the face to avoid skin atrophy and periorificial dermatitis.
- If the condition is severe, extensive, or refractory despite treatment, consider evaluating for immunosuppression (e.g., HIV testing) and referral to dermatology; allergic contact dermatitis to hair products should also be considered, with patch testing if refractory.
- Schedule follow-up in 4–6 weeks to assess response; advise earlier return if lesions worsen, signs of secondary infection develop, or new symptoms appear.
Notes: 
- Seborrheic dermatitis is chronic and may require maintenance therapy even after initial improvement.
- If no improvement after appropriate treatment, reconsider alternative diagnoses (e.g., tinea amiantacea, pediculosis, psoriasis, or contact dermatitis).
- Mild itching after showering may reflect water-induced irritation of the scalp barrier; gentle skin care is advised.

Vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after 6 days of persistent high fever unresponsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen. Over the past several days, she has noticed redness in both eyes without discharge, a rash on his trunk, swelling of his hands and feet, cracked bleeding lips, and a red bumpy tongue. Vignette:
A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after 6 days of persistent high fever unresponsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen. Over the past several days, she has noticed redness in both eyes without discharge, a rash on his trunk, swelling of his hands and feet, cracked bleeding lips, and a red bumpy tongue. He has been increasingly irritable and refusing to eat. On examination, the child is febrile, irritable, and difficult to console. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 148, RR 28, BP 86/52. Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection is present. Lips are erythematous with fissures. A prominent strawberry tongue is noted. A diffuse polymorphous maculopapular rash covers the trunk and perineum with early desquamation in the groin. Bilateral hands and feet show indurative edema with erythema. Right anterior cervical lymphadenopathy measuring 2.0 cm is palpable. Labs: WBC 18,600/mcL, ESR 82 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, platelets 488,000/mcL, ALT 68 U/L. Echocardiogram reveals dilated left anterior descending coronary artery (z-score 3.2). IVIG and high-dose aspirin are initiated.

Sex: Male

Analysis: The child meets the diagnostic criteria for complete Kawasaki disease: fever for more than 5 days plus all five principal clinical features (bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes including fissured lips and strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, extremity changes with indurative edema and erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy). Laboratory findings of leukocytosis (WBC 18,600/mcL), markedly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 82 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/dL), hypoalbuminemia (2.6 g/dL), thrombocytosis (platelets 488,000/mcL), and elevated ALT (68 U/L) support active systemic vasculitis. Echocardiographic demonstration of a dilated left anterior descending coronary artery (z-score 3.2) confirms cardiac involvement and mandates urgent intervention. Differential diagnoses include viral infections (measles, adenovirus), bacterial infections (scarlet fever, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, toxic shock syndrome), drug reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C); however, the full constellation of clinical features with coronary artery dilation most strongly favors Kawasaki disease.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Repeat echocardiography at 1–2 weeks and 4–6 weeks after treatment (more frequently if abnormalities persist or fever continues); baseline electrocardiogram; urinalysis for sterile pyuria; blood cultures to exclude bacterial infection; SARS-CoV-2 testing to rule out MIS-C; baseline coagulation profile in anticipation of possible anticoagulation; assessment of IVIG resistance predictors (low albumin, high neutrophil count, young age).
Conclusion: This 3-year-old boy presents with complete Kawasaki disease complicated by coronary artery dilation (LAD z-score 3.2). The persistent fever, severe systemic inflammation, and active cardiac involvement constitute an emergent situation requiring immediate treatment with IVIG and high-dose aspirin to prevent progression to coronary artery aneurysm, thrombosis, and myocardial infarction. Prompt recognition and therapy are critical to improve outcomes.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Administer IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion and initiate high-dose aspirin (30–50 mg/kg/day, or 80–100 mg/kg/day divided q6h per some protocols) for anti-inflammatory effect; transition to low-dose aspirin (3–5 mg/kg/day) for antiplatelet effect once fever resolves. If fever persists or recurs more than 36 hours after IVIG completion, consider a second IVIG dose, corticosteroids, or adjunctive therapy (infliximab, anakinra) given the 10–20% IVIG resistance rate and its association with higher coronary aneurysm risk. Provide supportive care for severe mucositis (irritability and refusal to eat), maintain adequate hydration, and monitor vital signs and cardiac status. Arrange pediatric cardiology co-management with serial echocardiography at 1–2 weeks and 4–6 weeks, and long-term cardiovascular follow-up stratified by z-score categories. Monitor for associated findings including hepatitis, aseptic meningitis, gallbladder hydrops, sterile pyuria, and arthritis. Assess for recent SARS-CoV-2 infection or exposure and obtain family history of vasculitis or coronary artery disease. Consider aspirin-related Reye syndrome risk with influenza or varicella exposure; defer live vaccines for 11 months after high-dose aspirin/IVIG therapy. Educate caregivers on signs of cardiac ischemia and the need for prompt evaluation of any recurrent fever.
Notes: Thrombocytosis (platelets 488,000/mcL) will likely peak in weeks 2–3 and contributes to thrombotic risk, warranting monitoring. Low albumin and elevated ALT indicate more severe systemic inflammation and possible hepatic involvement. Coronary artery abnormalities determine long-term cardiovascular risk, follow-up intensity, activity restrictions, and antithrombotic strategy. MIS-C should remain in consideration if cardiac dysfunction, gastrointestinal symptoms, or elevated troponin/BNP emerge, though this presentation is most consistent with classic Kawasaki disease.

Age: 30
Sex: Male
Complaint: Dull ache in the right wrist, gradually worsening over the past 2 weeks, aggravated by prolonged gaming sessions and relieved by rest. No history of specific injury, swelling, numbness, or locking. Right-hand dominant.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with an overuse tendinopathy of the dorsal extensor tendons of the wrist, likely extensor carpi radialis tendinopathy or intersection syndrome. Supporting facts include the gradual onset of dull pain in a repetitive-activity setting (avid gamer), tenderness localized along the dorsal extensor tendons without visible swelling or erythema, full range of motion, negative Finkelstein test, and intact neurovascular exam. The mildly reduced grip strength compared to the left suggests early functional impairment from pain or tendon irritation. Red flags are absent: no trauma, no signs of infection (no erythema, swelling, or fever), no neurovascular deficit, and no mechanical locking. Main differential considerations include De Quervain's tenosynovitis (less likely given negative Finkelstein), intersection syndrome, extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy, dorsal wrist ganglion cyst, scaphoid stress fracture, early wrist osteoarthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome (unlikely given absence of numbness), and inflammatory arthritis. Serious causes such as septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, fracture, or neurovascular compromise are considered but deemed unlikely based on the history and examination.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. No imaging or laboratory tests are indicated initially, as the diagnosis is clinical. Plain radiographs of the wrist may be considered if symptoms persist beyond 4–6 weeks of conservative management or if fracture is suspected. Ultrasound can be considered for tendon pathology if the diagnosis remains uncertain or symptoms are refractory.
Conclusion: This is a non-emergent overuse tendinopathy of the dorsal extensor tendons of the right wrist, consistent with repetitive strain from prolonged gaming. The condition is benign in presentation with no red flags, and conservative management is appropriate as the initial approach.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Initiate conservative management: activity modification (limit or reduce prolonged gaming sessions), rest, ice, and NSAIDs or acetaminophen for pain control. Use a wrist splint or brace during aggravating activities, and refer to hand-focused physical or occupational therapy for stretching and strengthening exercises. Perform an ergonomic assessment of the gaming setup, including keyboard, mouse, wrist position, desk height, and chair height, and recommend ergonomic adjustments (e.g., wrist support, neutral wrist position). Educate the patient on taking frequent breaks during gaming sessions and performing wrist stretching exercises. Specifically localize dorsal tenderness (1st vs. 2nd vs. 6th dorsal compartment) to narrow the exact tendon involved, and assess for crepitus during wrist extension to help differentiate intersection syndrome from simple tenosynovitis. winner_protocol:
Age: 48 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Nasal-sounding voice with air escaping through the nose during speech, first noticed one week after balloon rhinoplasty one year ago and progressively worsening over the last 3 months; voice is better in the morning and worse later in the day, with occasional nasal regurgitation of liquids but no dysphagia.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for myasthenia gravis (MG) with bulbar and ocular involvement. The strongest supporting facts include: fatigable nasal voice (better in the morning, worse later in the day), nasal regurgitation of liquids indicating palatal weakness, minimal left ptosis only with sustained upward gaze, and a decremental response to 3-Hz repetitive nerve stimulation in the left median and accessory nerves, with less pronounced decrement after 10 seconds of exercise (facilitation) and more pronounced decrement after 60 seconds (postfacilitation exhaustion)—a pattern characteristic of a postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder. The serum acetylcholine receptor antibody titer of 0.28 nmol/L (normal <0.02 nmol/L) provides strong serological confirmation. The differential diagnosis includes velopharyngeal insufficiency from prior surgery, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, bulbar-onset ALS, and brainstem lesions; however, the electrophysiological and serological findings are diagnostic of MG. The temporal relationship to surgery likely reflects unmasking of pre-existing MG by surgical stress rather than a direct surgical complication, given the progressive course and confirmatory testing.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest CT or MRI to evaluate for thymoma or thymic hyperplasia; pulmonary function tests (forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force) to assess respiratory reserve and baseline for crisis monitoring; consider single-fiber EMG for higher sensitivity and anti-MuSK antibody testing if AChR antibodies were equivocal; baseline serum electrolytes and renal function before initiating immunosuppression.

Conclusion: Myasthenia gravis with bulbar and ocular involvement, confirmed by characteristic EMG findings and elevated acetylcholine receptor antibody titer. The patient is clinically stable without respiratory compromise but requires prompt outpatient neurology evaluation and treatment to prevent progression.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations: Initiate an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (pyridostigmine) titrated to symptom control for rapid symptomatic relief. Arrange prompt neurology follow-up for consideration of immunosuppressive therapy (e.g., low-dose prednisone or steroid-sparing agents such as azathioprine or mycophenolate) for generalized disease. Refer for thymic imaging (CT chest) and surgical evaluation for thymectomy if a thymoma is identified, as thymectomy is indicated regardless of MG severity in that setting. Educate the patient on myasthenic crisis warning signs—new or worsening dyspnea, shortness of breath at rest, difficulty swallowing solids, choking, or neck weakness—and provide an action plan for emergency evaluation. Counsel the patient to avoid medications that exacerbate MG, including aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides (noting her erythromycin allergy), beta-blockers, magnesium, and botulinum toxin. Assess baseline pulmonary function (FVC, NIF) and monitor for impending respiratory failure, as bulbar symptoms increase aspiration risk. Address the left occipital shooting pains with further characterization, as they may represent occipital neuralgia or cervical pathology unrelated to MG. Given the patient is a woman of reproductive age, discuss pregnancy planning, as MG can worsen during pregnancy and certain immunosuppressants are contraindicated. Monitor for steroid side effects given her existing inhaled corticosteroid use for asthma. Perform a thorough autoimmune review, as MG can be associated with other autoimmune diseases.

Notes: Absence of diplopia, dysphagia, and limb weakness does not exclude MG, as the presentation can be purely bulbar and ocular initially. Minimal ptosis only with sustained upward gaze is a subtle but important finding supporting MG; monitor for progression to diplopia or worsening ptosis. The balloon rhinoplasty may have altered nasal anatomy or velopharyngeal function, but the EMG and serologic findings confirm neuromuscular junction dysfunction as the primary cause. The left occipital shooting pains may be unrelated to MG but warrant further evaluation.

winner_protocol:
Age: 58 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: A 58-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling of her right foot, following a nail puncture wound sustained 4 days prior while walking barefoot in her yard. She reports low-grade fever and mild chills. Examination reveals a plantar puncture wound with surrounding erythema extending 6 cm, warmth, edema, and tenderness; no crepitus or fluctuance; diminished peripheral pulses bilaterally. Last tetanus booster was over 10 years ago.

Analysis: This patient presents with a diabetic foot infection following a contaminated puncture wound. The key clinical concerns are the risk of rapidly progressive soft tissue infection, deep abscess, osteomyelitis, and potential limb-threatening complications. Supporting facts include the presence of diabetes mellitus (a major risk factor for impaired healing and increased susceptibility to infection), the puncture mechanism with outdoor exposure (raising concern for Pseudomonas and anaerobic organisms), spreading cellulitis (erythema extending 6 cm), systemic signs of infection (fever 100.6°F, chills), and diminished peripheral pulses bilaterally (suggesting underlying peripheral arterial disease that may compromise perfusion and response to therapy). The absence of crepitus or fluctuance does not exclude deep infection, particularly in a diabetic patient. Differential considerations include cellulitis, deep abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, retained foreign body, and necrotizing soft tissue infection. Given the combination of diabetes, systemic symptoms, spreading erythema, and vascular compromise, this warrants emergent evaluation and management.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Plain radiographs of the right foot (to evaluate for foreign body, gas, or osteomyelitis); laboratory work-up including complete blood count, C-reactive protein/erythrocyte sedimentation rate, blood glucose, renal function, and blood cultures (given systemic signs); consideration of MRI if deep infection or osteomyelitis is suspected despite normal plain films; vascular assessment (ankle-brachial index or Doppler studies) given diminished pulses.

Conclusion: This is a diabetic foot infection following a contaminated puncture wound in a patient with systemic signs of infection and evidence of peripheral vascular disease. The patient requires emergent care for evaluation of deep infection, initiation of broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, glycemic management, and urgent surgical consultation to assess for debridement, drainage, or retained foreign body. Delays in treatment risk progression to osteomyelitis, abscess, or limb-threatening complications.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease

Recommendations:
1. Admit the patient for inpatient management given diabetes, fever, spreading cellulitis, and diminished pulses; IV antibiotics are appropriate.
2. Initiate empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram-positive organisms (including MRSA), gram-negative organisms, Pseudomonas (given puncture mechanism and outdoor exposure), and anaerobes. Adjust based on culture results and clinical response.
3. Obtain urgent surgical consultation (general, orthopedic, or foot surgery) to assess for need for debridement, drainage, or exploration for retained foreign body. Note that diabetics may have deep infection without obvious surface signs such as fluctuance.
4. Administer tetanus prophylaxis: tetanus toxoid is indicated given the booster was over 10 years ago and the wound was contaminated; consider tetanus immune globulin (TIG) depending on prior vaccination history.
5. Obtain imaging and labs as listed above; MRI is most sensitive for osteomyelitis if deep infection is suspected.
6. Assess glycemic control and adjust insulin or oral agents during the acute infection; hyperglycemia impairs immune function and wound healing.
7. Evaluate for peripheral vascular disease and obtain vascular consultation given diminished pulses bilaterally; this impacts healing and may require revascularization.
8. Classify the diabetic foot infection severity (e.g., IDSA/IWGDF classification) to guide management and disposition.
9. Establish a follow-up plan with clear criteria for escalation (worsening systemic signs, spreading cellulitis, necrosis, crepitus) and provide wound care instructions and diabetic foot care education.
10. Refer to infectious disease, podiatry, wound care, and vascular surgery specialists as appropriate for ongoing management.

Notes: The absence of crepitus or fluctuance does not rule out deep infection or necrotizing process in a diabetic patient; maintain a low threshold for surgical exploration and advanced imaging. Monitor for progression of infection and vascular compromise closely. None other specified.

winner_protocol:
Age: 28

Sex: Female

Complaint: A 28-year-old woman, 3 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding, presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling in the right breast, associated with fever, chills, and malaise. She reports right-sided nipple soreness and cracking with difficulty latching. Examination reveals a wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, exquisitely tender, without fluctuance or palpable abscess, a small ipsilateral nipple fissure, and mildly enlarged right axillary lymph nodes.

Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for acute lactational (puerperal) mastitis. The strongest supporting facts are the postpartum breastfeeding status, the presence of a nipple fissure with latch difficulty (a known portal of entry for skin flora and a cause of milk stasis), the acute onset of localized wedge-shaped erythema, warmth, induration, and exquisite tenderness, and the systemic symptoms of fever (101.2°F) and chills. The patient is hemodynamically stable (HR 94, BP 118/72) with no fluctuance or palpable abscess, arguing against an established abscess and against an emergent condition. Main differential considerations include breast abscess (the most common complication of mastitis, which may be occult and not yet fluctuant), plugged duct, engorgement, galactocele, breast cellulitis unrelated to lactation, and inflammatory breast carcinoma (a rare but important mimic of persistent unilateral breast inflammation). The absence of a palpable mass and the presence of systemic symptoms favor infectious mastitis, but abscess and malignancy must be considered if the response to treatment is poor.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: The diagnosis is primarily clinical; no immediate additional testing is required. If an abscess is suspected or if there is no improvement within 48–72 hours, a breast ultrasound is indicated to differentiate cellulitis from a fluid-filled abscess and to guide drainage if needed. A CBC with differential may be obtained to assess leukocytosis if the patient appears more systemically ill. Milk culture is optional and may be useful in recurrent or severe cases. No routine mammography is needed in this young lactating woman without a suspicious mass.

Conclusion: This is acute lactational mastitis of the right breast in a stable postpartum patient, without evidence of abscess or sepsis. It requires non-emergent but prompt evaluation and outpatient management with antibiotics, continued milk removal, and supportive measures, with close follow-up to ensure resolution and to detect complications such as abscess formation.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology

Recommendations: Start empiric oral antibiotics targeting Staphylococcus aureus (e.g., dicloxacillin or cephalexin; consider clindamycin if MRSA is suspected). Continue breastfeeding or pumping from the affected breast to ensure milk removal and prevent stasis and abscess formation. Apply warm compresses and use analgesics/antipyretics (e.g., ibuprofen) for pain and fever. Ensure adequate hydration. Educate the patient on proper latch technique and nipple care, including hand hygiene and nipple ointment (e.g., lanolin), and refer to a lactation consultant to address the underlying latch difficulty and nipple fissure. Advise the patient to monitor temperature and breast symptoms, and to return immediately if fever persists beyond 48 hours, pain worsens, a fluctuant area develops, or signs of sepsis appear (e.g., hypotension, tachycardia out of proportion, altered mental status, rigors). Schedule a follow-up visit in 2–3 days to reassess for improvement; if there is no improvement within 48–72 hours, obtain breast ultrasound to rule out occult abscess and reconsider alternative diagnoses, including inflammatory breast carcinoma.

Notes: None

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

Vignette:
A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 8 presents with 2 days of worsening nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and progressive lethargy. She reports that she ran out of insulin 3 days ago and could not afford a refill. On examination, she is drowsy but arousable, markedly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 128, RR 32 (deep, labored Kussmaul respirations), BP 92/54, SpO2 99%. Her breath has a distinct fruity acetone odor. Abdomen is diffusely tender without peritoneal signs. Labs: glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.08, pCO2 14 mmHg, bicarbonate 4 mEq/L, anion gap 32, beta-hydroxybutyrate 8.2 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L (expected to drop with treatment), sodium 128 mEq/L (corrected 134), BUN 38 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL.
winner_protocol:
Age: 22 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Two days of worsening nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and progressive lethargy in a young woman with type 1 diabetes who ran out of insulin 3 days ago due to inability to afford a refill.

Analysis: The clinical picture is consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) precipitated by insulin omission. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of hyperglycemia (glucose 486 mg/dL), severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.08, bicarbonate 4 mEq/L, anion gap 32), and ketonemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate 8.2 mmol/L). The patient exhibits classic compensatory Kussmaul respirations (RR 32, deep and labored) and a fruity acetone odor. She is markedly dehydrated (dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor) and has altered mental status (drowsy but arousable, progressive lethargy), with hemodynamic instability (HR 128, BP 92/54) suggesting significant volume depletion. The initial potassium of 5.6 mEq/L is expected to drop with insulin and fluid therapy, and the sodium of 128 mEq/L corrects to 134 mEq/L for hyperglycemia. Elevated BUN and creatinine reflect prerenal azotemia from dehydration. The main differential considerations include other causes of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (e.g., lactic acidosis, toxic ingestions), but the combination of hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and the classic clinical presentation firmly establishes DKA. The underlying social determinant — inability to afford insulin — is a critical precipitating factor that must be addressed to prevent recurrence.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Bedside glucose monitoring (hourly), continuous cardiac monitoring, point-of-care or serial venous blood gas for pH and pCO2, serial serum electrolytes (particularly potassium), serum beta-hydroxybutyrate, renal function tests, and urine or serum ketone measurement. No additional imaging or studies are indicated at this time.

Conclusion: This is severe diabetic ketoacidosis with altered mental status and hemodynamic compromise, requiring emergent care and intensive monitoring. Management must include aggressive fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion, and careful potassium replacement, with attention to the social barrier of insulin affordability to prevent recurrent DKA.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Recommendations: Admit to an intensive care unit (ICU) given severe acidosis (pH 7.08), altered mental status, and hemodynamic instability. Initiate IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline at 15–20 mL/kg in the first hour, then reassess. Begin IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr once serum potassium is confirmed >3.3 mEq/L; do not give a bolus if potassium is low. Replace potassium once serum K drops below 5.2 mEq/L, anticipating a rapid decline with insulin and fluid therapy. Monitor glucose hourly and add dextrose to IV fluids when glucose reaches approximately 200 mg/dL to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin to close the anion gap. Monitor electrolytes, acid–base status, and mental status frequently. Address the precipitating social determinant: consult social work, connect the patient to insulin assistance programs, and provide education on sick-day management and DKA warning signs. Arrange outpatient endocrinology follow-up and ensure a discharge plan that secures insulin affordability.

Notes: The initial hyperkalemia (5.6 mEq/L) is expected to fall with treatment; avoid potassium replacement until levels drop below 5.2 mEq/L. Corrected sodium is 134 mEq/L, reflecting dilution from hyperglycemia. Monitor for complications including hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, and cerebral edema, though the latter is less common in adults. None.

Vignette: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back between his shoulder blades that began 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy boxes. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and takes amlodipine intermittently. On examination, he is writhing in pain and appears ashen. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 210/118 in the right arm and 162/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is auscultated along the left sternal border. Pulses are diminished in the left upper extremity. Chest X-ray shows widened mediastinum. CT angiography of the chest reveals a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch.

The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
