Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 32 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Painless vaginal bleeding at 36 weeks gestation that progressed to heavier bright-red bleeding with uterine cramping and non-reassuring fetal heart rate tracing.

Analysis: The patient presented with painless vaginal bleeding at 36 weeks gestation. Initial evaluation showed a fundal placenta with margins clear of the cervical os on ultrasound, effectively ruling out placenta previa. The initial fetal tracing was reactive. However, within one hour, the patient developed irregular cramping and contractions, increased bright-red vaginal bleeding (~50 cc), and the fetal monitor demonstrated uterine irritability with recurrent late decelerations and minimal-to-absent variability, indicating significant fetal compromise. Internal exam showed progressive cervical dilation from 1 cm to 3 cm with 50% effacement and station -3. The combination of new-onset contractions, progressive cervical change, increasing vaginal bleeding, and ominous fetal heart rate abnormalities in a patient with a fundal placenta is classic for acute placental abruption. Maternal smoking (2 cigarettes/day) is a known risk factor for placental abruption. The differential diagnosis includes vasa previa, uterine rupture, cervical/vaginal lesions, bloody show, and coagulopathy; however, the fundal placental location, absence of prior uterine surgery, normal coagulation labs, and the acute fetal deterioration make placental abruption the most likely diagnosis. The patient is A+ (Rh positive) and the Kleihauer-Betke test was negative, so Rh immunoglobulin is not indicated.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring; repeat bedside ultrasound to assess for retroplacental clot; repeat hemoglobin/hematocrit and coagulation panel (PT/PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) if bleeding worsens; type and crossmatch for blood products; large-bore IV access; oxygen delivery equipment; equipment for emergency cesarean delivery; neonatal resuscitation team availability.

Conclusion: This is an acute obstetric emergency consistent with placental abruption at 36 weeks gestation complicated by fetal distress (recurrent late decelerations, minimal/absent variability) and ongoing hemorrhage. Immediate delivery is required, most safely by cesarean section given the patient is only 3 cm dilated at station -3. Maternal stabilization with IV access, fluid resuscitation, and blood product availability is essential, with neonatal team notification for the late-preterm infant.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology

Recommendations: 1) Admit to labor and delivery with continuous electronic fetal monitoring. 2) Establish two large-bore IV lines and administer oxygen by mask. 3) Prepare for immediate emergency cesarean delivery given fetal distress and unfavorable cervical status (3 cm dilated, station -3). 4) Notify obstetric anesthesia and neonatology teams for delivery attendance. 5) Obtain type and crossmatch for blood products; ensure availability for potential transfusion. 6) Repeat bedside ultrasound to evaluate for retroplacental clot. 7) Repeat hemoglobin/hematocrit and coagulation studies to monitor for hemorrhage and DIC. 8) Keep patient NPO and obtain informed consent for cesarean delivery, explaining the urgency, risks of preterm birth versus continued pregnancy, and planned interventions. 9) Rh immunoglobulin is not required as the patient is A+ (Rh positive) with a negative Kleihauer-Betke test. 10) Betamethasone administration is optional at 36 weeks if delivery can be briefly delayed, but given fetal distress, immediate delivery takes priority. 11) Monitor maternal vital signs, urine output, and signs of hemodynamic compromise; be prepared for postpartum hemorrhage management.

Notes: Ultrasound has limited sensitivity for detecting placental abruption; a negative scan does not exclude the diagnosis. The patient's prenatal records are unavailable, and her Rh status was initially unknown but has been confirmed as A+ (Rh positive). Maternal smoking is a contributing risk factor for abruption. The fetal heart rate abnormalities (late decelerations with minimal/absent variability) are ominous and mandate urgent delivery.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.

The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.

- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man who is an avid hiker in Connecticut presents with a 5-day history of an expanding red rash on his right thigh that he noticed after a weekend camping trip two weeks ago. He recalls removing an engorged tick from his thigh. He now reports fatigue, mild headache, arthralgias in his knees and wrists, and low-grade fever. He denies neck stiffness, facial weakness, chest pain, or palpitations. On examination, temperature is 99.6°F. There is a 12 cm annular erythematous plaque on the right anterior thigh with central clearing, consistent with erythema migrans. There are no secondary skin lesions. Joints are nontender without effusion. Neurological examination is nonfocal. Heart rate is regular at 74 with no murmurs. There is no cervical rigidity.
winner_protocol:
Age: 35
Sex: Male
Complaint: Expanding red rash on the right thigh with fatigue, mild headache, arthralgias in knees and wrists, and low-grade fever, following a tick bite during a camping trip two weeks prior.
Analysis: The patient presents with a classic erythema migrans rash (12 cm annular erythematous plaque with central clearing) on the right thigh, a history of an engorged tick bite in an endemic area (Connecticut), and systemic symptoms (fatigue, headache, arthralgias, low-grade fever). These findings are consistent with early localized Lyme disease. The absence of neck stiffness, facial weakness, cardiac symptoms, secondary skin lesions, joint effusion, and focal neurological deficits argues against disseminated disease. The main differential considerations include other tick-borne infections (anaplasmosis, babesiosis), cellulitis, tinea corporis, Southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI), hypersensitivity reactions, erythema multiforme, and granuloma annulare. The clinical picture is unequivocal, and the patient is stable without red flags for complications, supporting non-emergent outpatient management.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Diagnosis is clinical; serologic testing is not required for typical erythema migrans but may be considered if the diagnosis is uncertain. Baseline laboratory studies (CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel/liver function tests) may be obtained to assess for co-infections. A resting ECG can be considered to screen for silent Lyme carditis. Treatment should not be delayed pending results.
Conclusion: Early localized Lyme disease with erythema migrans in a stable patient. The patient requires prompt outpatient antibiotic therapy and monitoring for signs of dissemination, but no emergent intervention is indicated.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Initiate oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10–21 days as first-line therapy; alternatives include amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily if doxycycline is contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy, allergy, children <8 years). Counsel on doxycycline photosensitivity. Instruct the patient to complete the full course, monitor for resolution of rash and symptoms, and return promptly if new neurological (meningitis, facial palsy, radiculopathy), cardiac (palpitations, chest pain, syncope), or joint symptoms develop. Schedule follow-up in 2–4 weeks to assess treatment efficacy. Educate on tick avoidance, proper tick removal, and symptom monitoring given the patient's hiking activity. Consider co-infection with anaplasmosis or babesiosis if fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or hemolysis are present. Warn about a possible Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within 24 hours of starting therapy. Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated since erythema migrans is already present. Assess immunocompetence status as it may affect severity and treatment duration.
Notes: Serologic testing is insensitive in the first few weeks of infection and should not delay treatment; it may be useful later if symptoms persist or disseminated disease is suspected. A baseline ECG can be considered because Lyme carditis may be asymptomatic initially. Geographic prevalence in Connecticut supports the diagnosis.

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. Vignette:
A 6-week-old male infant is brought in by his parents who are concerned about episodes of inconsolable crying that occur most evenings. The crying episodes last 2 to 3 hours, during which the baby draws up his knees and appears to be in distress. The episodes typically begin around 6 PM and resolve by bedtime. Between episodes, the infant is calm and content. He is exclusively breastfed, feeding well, and gaining weight along the 50th percentile. He has no fever, vomiting, or bloody stools. On examination, the infant is calm and alert. Abdomen is soft and non-distended with normal bowel sounds. Fontanelles are flat. The exam is entirely normal.
winner_protocol:
Age: 6 weeks
Sex: Male
Complaint: Episodes of inconsolable crying occurring most evenings, lasting 2–3 hours, with the infant drawing up his knees and appearing distressed; episodes begin around 6 PM and resolve by bedtime, with the infant calm and content between episodes.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for infantile colic. The 6-week-old male infant meets the "rule of threes" (crying more than 3 hours per day, more than 3 days per week, for more than 3 weeks) with paroxysmal evening crying, drawing up of knees, and a completely normal physical examination. Strong supporting facts include exclusive breastfeeding with adequate intake, weight gain along the 50th percentile, absence of fever, vomiting, or bloody stools, and a soft, non-distended abdomen with normal bowel sounds and flat fontanelles. These findings argue against organic pathology. Main differential considerations include gastroesophageal reflux, cow's milk protein allergy, intussusception, urinary tract infection, otitis media, constipation, hair tourniquet syndrome, corneal abrasion, and non-accidental injury; all are excluded by the normal history and physical exam in this case. The condition is self-limiting, peaks at 6 weeks of age, and typically resolves by 3–4 months.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. No laboratory or imaging studies are indicated for classic colic without red flags; the diagnosis is clinical.
Conclusion: This is a case of infantile colic in a thriving 6-week-old male infant. The presentation is non-urgent, benign, and self-limiting, with a normal physical examination and no red flags. Management centers on parental reassurance, education, and supportive soothing techniques, with ongoing monitoring for resolution by 3–4 months of age and vigilance for any evolving organic pathology.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations:
- Provide parental reassurance and education that colic is a common, self-limiting condition that typically resolves by 3–4 months of age; emphasize that the infant is healthy and thriving.
- Advise soothing techniques including swaddling, white noise, rocking, and use of a pacifier; review feeding and burping technique to address overfeeding, underfeeding, or improper burping.
- Consider a trial of probiotics (e.g., Lactobacillus reuteri) or simethicone, acknowledging limited and variable evidence; avoid unnecessary medications without clear benefit.
- If atypical features or a strong family history of atopy/allergy are present, consider a 2–4 week trial of extensively hydrolyzed formula or maternal dairy elimination; exclusive breastfeeding does not exclude colic, and maternal diet (e.g., cow's milk, caffeine) may be a contributing factor.
- Assess parental coping and stress, and provide support resources; address parental anxiety to prevent shaken baby syndrome.
- Recommend documentation of a crying diary to quantify episodes and identify triggers or patterns.
- Schedule routine well-child visits and monitor for resolution by 3–4 months of age; instruct parents to return promptly if red flags develop (fever, persistent vomiting, bloody stools, poor weight gain, lethargy, abdominal distension, abnormal fontanelle, abnormal vital signs, or signs of trauma).
- During examination, specifically check for hair tourniquet syndrome (fingers, toes, penis), corneal abrasion, and occult fractures, which can present as inconsolable crying.
Notes: The infant's normal weight percentile and adequate feeding argue against malabsorption or significant reflux. Prolonged crying (>3 hours) in an otherwise healthy infant is still considered colic unless red flags appear. None.

Vignette:
A 27-year-old woman with a history of moderate persistent asthma presents to the emergency room with progressive worsening of shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough over 3 days. She reports prior exposure to a person who had a runny nose and a hacking cough. She did not receive significant relief from her rescue inhaler with worsening symptoms, despite increased use. She has been compliant with her maintenance asthma regimen, which consists of an inhaled corticosteroid and a leukotriene receptor antagonist for maintenance therapy and albuterol as rescue therapy. Her cough is disrupting her sleep pattern and as a consequence she is experiencing daytime somnolence, which is affecting her job performance.
winner_protocol:
Age: 27

Sex: Female

Complaint: Progressive worsening of shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough over 3 days in a woman with moderate persistent asthma, with poor response to increased rescue inhaler use, sleep disruption, and daytime somnolence affecting job performance.

Analysis: The patient has a known history of moderate persistent asthma and presents with a classic acute asthma exacerbation. The most likely trigger is a viral upper respiratory infection, given her recent exposure to a person with rhinorrhea and a hacking cough. Strong supporting facts include the progressive nature of dyspnea, wheezing, and cough; the lack of significant relief from her rescue albuterol despite increased use; and the impact on sleep and daytime function, which indicates a moderate-to-severe exacerbation beyond self-care. The daytime somnolence raises concern for possible hypoxemia or hypercapnia and warrants urgent evaluation. Main differential considerations include viral bronchitis/tracheobronchitis, community-acquired pneumonia, COVID-19 or other respiratory viral infections, and less likely pulmonary embolism, vocal cord dysfunction, cardiac causes, or anaphylaxis. These mimics should be considered, particularly if atypical features are present.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pulse oximetry; peak expiratory flow rate (or bedside spirometry); chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia or pneumothorax; arterial blood gas if severe; and focused infectious work-up (e.g., respiratory viral panel, COVID-19/influenza testing) given the sick contact.

Conclusion: This is a moderate-to-severe acute asthma exacerbation, most likely triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection, in a patient with moderate persistent asthma who is failing rescue therapy. She requires emergent evaluation and treatment to prevent respiratory compromise, with subsequent optimization of her chronic asthma management.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology

Recommendations: Initiate emergent management: administer supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO₂ ≥ 94%; give repeated or continuous nebulized short-acting beta-agonists (albuterol); add ipratropium bromide; start systemic corticosteroids (e.g., oral prednisone 40–60 mg or IV methylprednisolone); consider IV magnesium sulfate if response is suboptimal; and monitor response with serial peak flow measurements and vital signs. Assess for signs of impending respiratory failure (inability to speak in full sentences, accessory muscle use, silent chest, altered mental status, cyanosis, SpO₂ < 90%) and escalate to ICU if present. If influenza is identified, consider antiviral therapy. After stabilization, likely admission or observation is warranted given the severity and lack of response to rescue therapy. On discharge, re-educate inhaler technique, step-up controller therapy (e.g., increase inhaled corticosteroid dose or add a long-acting beta-agonist), assess need for oral steroid taper, consider biologic therapy if frequent exacerbations, provide a written asthma action plan, and schedule follow-up with Pulmonology within 1–2 weeks. Address infection prevention measures given the viral trigger.

Notes: None

Age: 26 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Painful urination, feeling of urgent need to urinate, and more frequent urination for 2 days. Denies fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, back pain, vaginal discharge, or vaginal pruritus.  
Analysis: The patient presents with the classic triad of dysuria, urgency, and urinary frequency without any systemic symptoms (fever, chills, nausea, vomiting) or flank/back pain. This pattern strongly supports a diagnosis of acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection). Her newly wed status raises the possibility of "honeymoon cystitis" related to increased sexual activity, a recognized risk factor. The absence of fever, chills, and flank pain effectively rules out pyelonephritis. The absence of vaginal discharge and pruritus makes vaginitis unlikely. Main differential considerations include urethritis (including STI-related), vaginitis/cervicitis, interstitial cystitis, and overactive bladder; pelvic inflammatory disease and renal colic are less likely given the lack of systemic, vaginal, or flank symptoms but remain worth considering if the history changes. The condition is non-emergent and safely managed in an outpatient primary care setting.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urinalysis (dipstick) for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, blood, and protein; point-of-care pregnancy test before prescribing antibiotics; urine culture with sensitivity reserved for recurrent, persistent, atypical, or complicated cases, or if treatment fails.  
Conclusion: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection) in a 26-year-old newly wed female, consistent with possible honeymoon cystitis. No red flags for upper tract infection or complicated UTI are present. The condition is non-emergent and appropriate for outpatient management in General Medicine.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  
Recommendations:  
- Prescribe empirical oral antibiotics: nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID for 5 days, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 160/800 mg PO BID for 3 days if no sulfa allergy and local resistance is low.  
- Rule out pregnancy with a point-of-care test before prescribing, as some agents are contraindicated in pregnancy.  
- Advise increased fluid intake and adequate hydration; assess current hydration status.  
- Offer symptomatic relief with phenazopyridine or an NSAID as needed.  
- Counsel the patient to void after intercourse and maintain good hygiene to reduce recurrence risk.  
- Review contraceptive method; spermicides and diaphragms increase UTI risk and should be reconsidered.  
- Assess for prior UTI history, diabetes, immunosuppression, urinary tract anomalies, medication allergies (nitrofurantoin, sulfa), and potential STI exposure.  
- Consider screening for sexually transmitted infections (e.g., chlamydia, gonorrhea) if urethritis is suspected, despite the absence of vaginal symptoms.  
- Arrange follow-up reassessment in 48–72 hours if symptoms do not improve; investigate recurrent or persistent symptoms for anatomical abnormalities or recurrent UTI.  
- Educate on red flags (fever, chills, flank/back pain, nausea, vomiting, gross hematuria, signs of sepsis) that warrant urgent re-evaluation for possible pyelonephritis.  
Notes: Pregnancy must be excluded before antibiotic selection. Local antimicrobial resistance patterns should guide empiric choice. If symptoms persist or recur, urine culture and further urologic evaluation are indicated.

Age: 2 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Yellowish, greasy-appearing scales on the scalp present for approximately 2 weeks; scales are thick in some areas, with no rash elsewhere on the body.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for infantile seborrheic dermatitis (cradle cap). The strongest supporting facts are the adherent yellowish-white greasy scales over the anterior fontanelle and vertex of the scalp in a thriving 2-month-old infant with no underlying erythema, no oozing, no involvement of the face or diaper area, and no systemic symptoms. The infant is feeding well, gaining weight appropriately, and sleeping normally, which supports a benign, self-limited process. Main differential considerations include atopic dermatitis, tinea capitis, infantile psoriasis, and bacterial impetiginization; these are considered less likely given the absence of pruritus, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, hair loss or broken hairs, and systemic signs. Neonatal lupus and ichthyosis vulgaris are even less likely. The absence of involvement of the face, diaper area, or other skin folds makes generalized seborrheic dermatitis or Leiner's disease less likely. Thick scales may be mistaken for tinea capitis, but the absence of hair loss and broken hairs argues against it.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical; no routine diagnostic tests are indicated. If tinea capitis is suspected (e.g., hair loss, broken hairs, kerion), KOH preparation or fungal culture may be considered.
Conclusion: This is infantile seborrheic dermatitis (cradle cap), a benign, self-limited condition in a thriving infant. It does not require urgent medical care and can be managed conservatively with parental reassurance and education.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Manage with gentle washing using a mild shampoo, application of emollients (e.g., mineral oil or petroleum jelly) to soften the scales, and soft brushing to gently loosen and remove them. Avoid harsh scrubbing or vigorous removal of scales, especially over the open anterior fontanelle. Do not pick at the scales, as this can cause fissuring and secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization). Provide parental education and counseling to reduce anxiety and prevent excessive treatment with harsh shampoos or picking. Consider a low-potency topical steroid or topical antifungal only if inflammation or fungal infection appears (conditional). Reevaluate in 2–4 weeks if there is no improvement, or sooner if any red flag develops (fever, poor feeding, irritability, spreading rash, oozing/crusting, fissures/bleeding, neurologic signs, failure to thrive). Refer to dermatology for persistent, extensive, or atypical cases. Consider family history of atopy or psoriasis, which may influence the differential. If the condition is persistent, extensive, or associated with diarrhea, failure to thrive, or skin fragility, consider rare disorders such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis or zinc/biotin deficiency. Also consider recent use of new skin products or detergents, exposure to caregivers with active skin infections, immunodeficiency states, underlying scalp abnormalities, or recent antibiotic use as potential modifying factors.
Notes: Red flags that would prompt further evaluation include fever, poor feeding, spreading rash, oozing, crusting, failure to thrive, fissures/bleeding, irritability, and neurologic signs. Cradle cap typically peaks around 2–3 weeks to 3 months of age and resolves spontaneously as the infant's sebaceous glands mature and maternal hormonal influence wanes. There may be a possible association with later development of atopic disease, so monitoring for evolution into atopic dermatitis is reasonable. Seborrheic dermatitis in infants is often associated with Malassezia yeast, but treatment is symptomatic.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

[6]
tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

She reports mild rhinorrhea and fatigue. She did not receive the influenza vaccine this season. winner_protocol:
Age: 30
Sex: Female
Complaint: A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents with a 2-day history of high fever, body aches, headache, sore throat, dry nonproductive cough, mild rhinorrhea, and fatigue. She did not receive the influenza vaccine this season. Vital signs show temperature 101.8°F, heart rate 96, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Fundal height is consistent with gestational age and fetal heart tones are reassuring at 145 bpm. Rapid influenza antigen test is positive for influenza A. She has no signs of respiratory distress or dehydration.

Analysis: The patient presents with classic influenza-like symptoms (fever, body aches, headache, sore throat, dry cough, rhinorrhea, fatigue) and a positive rapid influenza antigen test for influenza A, confirming acute influenza A infection in a pregnant patient at 28 weeks gestation. The clinical picture is most consistent with uncomplicated influenza A. The patient is clinically stable: vital signs are reassuring (temperature 101.8°F, heart rate 96, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air), lungs are clear, fetal heart tones are reassuring at 145 bpm, and there are no signs of respiratory distress or dehydration. Pregnancy is a recognized risk factor for severe influenza, including higher rates of hospitalization, ICU admission, and mortality, so prompt antiviral therapy is critical. The patient is within the 48-hour window from symptom onset, when oseltamivir is most effective. Differential considerations include other viral respiratory infections (e.g., COVID-19, RSV, adenovirus), streptococcal pharyngitis, and bacterial pneumonia; although the positive rapid antigen test makes influenza A most likely, false positives and co-infections are possible. Secondary bacterial superinfection (e.g., pneumonia) should be considered if symptoms worsen after 5-7 days. The missed influenza vaccination represents a prevention opportunity for this and future seasons.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Confirmatory influenza PCR if rapid test result is in question; COVID-19 PCR given overlapping symptoms; baseline CBC and electrolytes to assess for leukocytosis or dehydration; fetal heart rate monitoring (already reassuring at 145 bpm). Chest X-ray with abdominal shielding is not currently indicated but should be considered if respiratory symptoms worsen or persistent high fever develops.

Conclusion: This is a 30-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks gestation with acute, uncomplicated influenza A infection. She is clinically stable with reassuring maternal vital signs, clear lungs, and reassuring fetal heart tones, and does not require emergent care. Management should be prompt, non-emergent care led by Obstetrics and Gynecology, with initiation of antiviral therapy (oseltamivir) within the 48-hour window, supportive care, and close monitoring for maternal and fetal red flags.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology

Recommendations:
- Initiate oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days as soon as possible; the patient is within the 48-hour window from symptom onset, when treatment is most effective. Oseltamivir is safe in pregnancy.
- Provide supportive care: adequate hydration, rest, and acetaminophen for fever and pain (preferred antipyretic in pregnancy; avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester). Treat maternal hyperthermia.
- Counsel on red flags requiring immediate return or escalation of care: respiratory distress, hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%), chest pain, persistent high fever (> 102°F or > 39.5°C), altered mental status, signs of dehydration, decreased fetal movement, or signs of preterm labor.
- Monitor for preterm labor, fetal distress, and adverse pregnancy outcomes; fetal heart tones are currently reassuring at 145 bpm, but ongoing fetal monitoring is warranted given increased risks associated with influenza in pregnancy.
- Re-evaluate in 48-72 hours (telehealth or office visit) to ensure response to antivirals and detect progression to severe disease.
- Consider co-infection with COVID-19 or other respiratory pathogens, especially in pandemic settings; test accordingly.
- Consider secondary bacterial superinfection (e.g., pneumonia) if symptoms worsen after 5-7 days; if persistent high fever develops, obtain chest X-ray with abdominal shielding.
- Address the missed vaccination opportunity: discuss seasonal influenza vaccination for the remainder of this pregnancy (if applicable) and postpartum vaccination; vaccination during pregnancy protects both mother and infant for up to 6 months after birth.
- Counsel close contacts regarding possible prophylactic antivirals or vaccination.
- Consider Infectious Disease consultation if the course becomes complicated.

Notes: Pregnancy is a risk factor for severe influenza, including higher rates of hospitalization, ICU admission, and mortality; maintain a low threshold for escalation of care. Maternal comorbidities (e.g., asthma, diabetes, obesity) would raise concern but are not present in this case. The patient should be advised to return immediately for shortness of breath, chest pain, confusion, or decreased fetal movement.

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.

A 22-year-old male college student presents with a painful sore inside his mouth for the past 2 days. He is in the middle of final examinations and reports increased stress and poor sleep. He denies fever, multiple ulcers, genital sores, or joint pain. He has no history of inflammatory bowel disease. winner_protocol:
Age: 22 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Painful sore inside the mouth for the past 2 days, occurring during a period of increased stress and poor sleep (final examinations). A single shallow oval ulcer (~5 mm) with a white-yellowish base and erythematous halo is present on the left buccal mucosa. No fever, multiple ulcers, genital sores, joint pain, or lymphadenopathy.

Analysis: The presentation is classic for a minor aphthous ulcer (canker sore). The strongest supporting facts are the single shallow oval ulcer with a white-yellowish base and erythematous halo on the buccal mucosa, the absence of systemic symptoms (no fever, genital sores, joint pain, or lymphadenopathy), and the presence of known precipitating factors (stress and poor sleep). The absence of lymphadenopathy and systemic features reduces concern for infectious or malignant causes. The absence of genital ulcers and joint pain helps exclude Behçet's disease. Main differential considerations include traumatic ulcer, herpes simplex virus ulcer, oral candidiasis, Behçet's disease, inflammatory bowel disease-associated oral ulcers, oral malignancy, syphilitic chancre, pemphigus vulgaris, and nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, folate). However, the classic morphology and lack of red flags strongly favor a minor aphthous ulcer. The condition is benign and self-limited, and no urgent evaluation is needed.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical. No diagnostic tests are indicated initially; testing (e.g., CBC, iron/B12/folate studies, viral PCR, biopsy) is reserved for atypical, persistent, or recurrent cases.

Conclusion: This is a minor aphthous ulcer (canker sore), a benign and self-limited condition. The patient can be managed conservatively with symptomatic relief, and no urgent medical evaluation is required. The ulcer is expected to heal within 7–10 days.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Recommendations:
- Reassure the patient that the ulcer is benign, not contagious, and should heal within 7–10 days.
- Provide symptomatic relief with topical anesthetics (e.g., benzocaine) and/or protective pastes; salt-water rinses may be helpful.
- Advise good oral hygiene and avoidance of irritants, including acidic/spicy foods, chocolate, nuts, and other dietary triggers.
- Recommend stress reduction and adequate sleep, as these are the identified precipitating factors in this case.
- Topical corticosteroids (e.g., triamcinolone acetonide in adhesive paste) may be considered for faster healing if pain is significant or if the ulcer persists beyond one week, but they are not strictly first-line for a minor ulcer.
- Advise the patient to return for evaluation if the ulcer does not heal within 2 weeks, worsens, or if new systemic symptoms develop (e.g., fever, multiple or recurrent ulcers, lymphadenopathy, severe pain, dysphagia, indurated or bleeding lesion).
- Consider screening for nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, folate), celiac disease, or HIV if ulcers become recurrent (>3–4 episodes/year), atypical, or severe.
- Review medication history for drugs that can cause oral ulceration (e.g., NSAIDs, beta-blockers, alendronate).
- Consider local trauma (cheek biting, sharp teeth, dental appliances) as a potential trigger and address if present.
- Note that smoking cessation can paradoxically trigger aphthous ulcers, while smoking may reduce frequency; this may be relevant for prevention counseling.
- If the ulcer persists beyond 2–3 weeks, consider biopsy to rule out malignancy or other pathology.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 68-year-old male farmer presents with a slowly growing lesion on his nose that he first noticed approximately 8 months ago. The lesion has gradually enlarged and occasionally bleeds when he washes his face but heals over. He has extensive sun exposure from decades of outdoor work and a history of multiple sunburns in his youth. He has never had skin cancer before. On examination, there is a 1.2 cm pearly, dome-shaped nodule on the left ala of the nose with a rolled border and central depression. Multiple telangiectasias are visible on the surface. The surrounding skin shows significant solar damage with actinic keratoses on the forehead and ears. There is no palpable cervical or preauricular lymphadenopathy. A dermoscopic examination reveals arborizing vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests.
winner_protocol:
Age: 68 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A 68-year-old male farmer presents with a slowly growing, pearly, dome-shaped nodule on the left ala of the nose, first noticed approximately 8 months ago. The lesion has gradually enlarged and occasionally bleeds when washing his face but heals over. He has extensive sun exposure from decades of outdoor work and a history of multiple sunburns in youth, with no prior history of skin cancer.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC). The pearly, dome-shaped nodule with rolled borders, central depression, and surface telangiectasias, combined with dermoscopic findings of arborizing vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests, are highly specific features of nodular BCC. The patient's extensive sun exposure, history of sunburns, and surrounding actinic keratoses on the forehead and ears support a diagnosis of chronic solar damage and field cancerization. The lesion is located on the nose, a high-risk (H-zone) anatomic site for BCC recurrence and local tissue destruction. The central depression may represent early ulceration, which can be a sign of more aggressive behavior. No cervical or preauricular lymphadenopathy is present, and there are no red flags such as rapid growth, neurological symptoms, or fixation to underlying structures, indicating a non-emergent but timely management approach. Differential considerations include squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma, amelanotic melanoma, sebaceous carcinoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, trichoepithelioma, sebaceous hyperplasia, fibrous papule, and less likely benign mimickers such as molluscum contagiosum or intradermal nevus; histopathology is required for definitive distinction.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin biopsy (punch or shave biopsy) of the lesion for histopathologic examination to confirm diagnosis and determine histologic subtype; full-body skin examination for additional lesions; dermoscopy (already performed). Imaging is not required unless deep invasion or perineural spread is suspected.
Conclusion: This is a suspected nodular basal cell carcinoma of the left ala of the nose in a patient with significant actinic damage. The lesion is locally invasive but slow-growing with low metastatic potential. Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation via biopsy, followed by surgical excision with margin control, preferably Mohs micrographic surgery given the cosmetically and functionally sensitive nasal location. The patient is at high risk for additional skin cancers and requires ongoing surveillance and sun protection counseling.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: 1) Refer promptly (within weeks) to Dermatology, preferably a team with Mohs micrographic surgery expertise, for biopsy and definitive treatment. 2) Perform a punch or shave biopsy of the lesion for histopathologic confirmation and histologic subtype determination (e.g., nodular vs. infiltrative/morpheaform/sclerosing, which are more aggressive). 3) Plan definitive treatment with Mohs micrographic surgery as first-line for tissue-sparing, high-cure-rate excision on the nose; standard surgical excision with appropriate margins is an acceptable alternative. Electrodessication and curettage is generally not recommended for this high-risk facial location. 4) Assess for red flags that would alter management: rapid growth, persistent ulceration or uncontrolled bleeding, pain, numbness/tingling/facial weakness (perineural invasion), fixation to underlying structures, regional lymphadenopathy, size >2 cm, or deep subcutaneous involvement. 5) Evaluate immunosuppressive status, family history of skin cancer (including Gorlin syndrome), prior radiation to head/neck, medication history (photosensitizing drugs, anticoagulants), and occupational chemical/pesticide exposure as potential co-factors. 6) Treat existing actinic keratoses on the forehead and ears. 7) Provide patient education on sun protection (broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, hat) and on warning signs such as bleeding, non-healing, or changes in the lesion. 8) Schedule regular full-body skin examinations at least annually (every 6-12 months) given the high risk for additional non-melanoma and melanoma skin cancers. 9) Plan for reconstructive considerations (flap or graft) after excision, addressing functional airway patency of the nasal ala and cosmetic outcomes. 10) Address psychosocial impact of the facial lesion and cosmetic concerns in patient counseling.
